Worth a go, if you’re in the area
Jun 2026 • Friends
Mama Masala has a very extensive menu, offering Northern and Southern Indian dishes. They also have a lot of Chinese dishes.

Important Information:
- The following is not advertised in the menu:
- All the food prices exclude 8% VAT.
- They don’t have beer in the menu, but they sell Saigon, Tiger and Heineken.
- If you order any alcohol, they will add 10% to the original price.
- Example: 1 x Can of Saigon is 45K, plus 10%, so the total price is 49,500

Taking the above into consideration, the prices are definitely on the higher side, especially for beer.

Service:
- The gentleman who greeted me when I walked in was welcoming and friendly.
- He listened to my requests, which was that my curry had no salt, and I didn’t want it floating in oil.
- Rating: 5/5

Atmosphere:
- During my visit they played some nice background music.

Indoors:
- To keep you cool, they have ceiling fans and air conditioning.
- Seating: Padded high-back wooden chairs.
- The lighting was good.

Outdoors:
- I didn’t see any portable fans.
- Seating: High-back plastic chairs. Not very comfortable.

Rating: 4/5

My Order:

- 1 x Chicken Chettinad
- Portion size: Good
- Great flavour, no oil or salt, but I wasn’t warned the chicken was on the bone, so when I took my first bite, I chipped one of my teeth on the bone.
- Price: 150K plus 8% vat
- Rating: 4/5

- 1 x Plain Rice:
- Portion size: Good
- The rice was served cold.
- I asked them to reheat it, which they did.
- Price: 30K plus 8% vat
- Rating: 4/5

- 1 x Plain Naan
- Portion size: Good
- This was one of the best naan’s I’ve tasted.
- It was light, fluffy, and tasted delicious.
- Price: 35K plus 8% vat
- Rating: 5/5

Additional Information:
They also provided complimentary water.
The toilets were clean and had tissue.

Overall Rating: 4/5

Mama Masala — Good Food, Frustrating Experience
May 2026 • Solo
The food at Mama Masala genuinely deserves praise. The flavors were well-developed, the spices layered thoughtfully, and the dishes arrived hot and fresh. On the culinary front, the kitchen is clearly doing something right.
However, the service experience left a lot to be desired and significantly dampened an otherwise promising meal.
Our order was brought out incorrectly — a basic error that happens, and one I’d normally overlook if handled with professionalism. What made it unacceptable was what followed. Rather than owning the mistake and correcting it, the staff member responsible — a gentleman wearing a cap and glasses — attempted to convince us that what was served was, in fact, what we’d ordered. It felt dismissive and, frankly, manipulative. No acknowledgment, no apology, no attempt to make it right.
In the hospitality business, how you recover from a mistake matters more than the mistake itself. A simple “I’m sorry, let me fix that” would have turned this into a non-issue.
Bottom line: The kitchen has real talent. But a restaurant is the full experience — food and service. Until the front-of-house culture aligns with the quality coming out of that kitchen, it’s hard to recommend wholeheartedly.
I hope management takes this as constructive feedback rather than just criticism. The potential here is real.
